explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves DONE_IN_PROC row-count messages enabled in usp_TestProcedure, increasing network and client overhead.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF prevents automatic transaction rollback on many runtime errors, risking partially applied transactions.
SELECT * on Sales.Orders retrieves unnecessary columns and tightly couples callers to table schema changes.
SELECT TOP (10) on Sales.Orders without an ORDER BY clause returns an arbitrary, nondeterministic set of rows.
DISTINCT is redundant because OrderID is already the primary key of Sales.Orders and guaranteed unique.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders allows dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, missing rows, or duplicate rows.
Applying YEAR(o.OrderDate) in the WHERE predicate prevents index range seeks and forces a scan on Sales.Orders.
Comparing int column o.CustomerID with nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText forces implicit conversion and can degrade index usage.
Using @CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID impairs cardinality estimation and prevents efficient index seeks on CustomerID.
The leading wildcard in o.Comments LIKE N'%urgent%' prevents index seeking and forces a full scan.
NOT IN against a subquery on Sales.Invoices can unexpectedly return zero rows if any subquery value is NULL.
Wrapping o.CustomerID in ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) makes the predicate non-sargable and prevents seeking on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID.
Performing arithmetic (o.OrderID + 0) in the predicate prevents an index seek on PK_Sales_Orders.
The inequality predicate o.CustomerID <> 1 is poorly selective and typically causes a broad scan of Sales.Orders.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate and produces a Cartesian product.
Comma-separated join syntax between Sales.Orders and Sales.OrderLines in FROM obscures join predicates and risks accidental Cartesian joins.
The correlated scalar subquery counting Sales.OrderLines executes per outer row of Sales.Orders instead of using a set-based join or aggregation.
The correlated EXISTS subquery on Sales.OrderLines evaluates per outer row instead of using a set-based join.
The CASE expression on o.Comments is duplicated in both the SELECT list and the ORDER BY clause.
ORDER BY 2 relies on select-list column position, which is fragile if columns are reordered or added.
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY orders only by non-unique o.OrderDate without a unique tie-breaker such as OrderID.
UNION performs unnecessary duplicate elimination between disjoint branches filtering o.OrderID = 1 and o.OrderID = 2.
Using SELECT COUNT(*) > 0 on Sales.OrderLines scans all matching rows when EXISTS would stop at the first match.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID FROM Sales.Orders silently overwrites @OrderID with an arbitrary last row when multiple rows match.
Using table variable @OrderIds can lead to inaccurate cardinality estimates and suboptimal query plans.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates a temporary table implicitly and holds schema locks in tempdb during population.
Declaring and iterating order_cursor processes Sales.Orders row by row instead of using a set-based operation.
The WHILE loop performs iterative row-by-row style processing rather than a set-based operation.
Concatenating @CustomerID into @Sql creates ad-hoc dynamic SQL strings instead of parameterized execution.
EXEC sys.sp_executesql @Sql executes dynamic SQL without parameterized inputs, preventing plan reuse.
Temporary table #Scratch is explicitly created with CREATE TABLE but never dropped before the procedure ends.
The CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE() and neither rethrows with THROW nor returns an error status, hiding runtime failures.
RAISERROR is used instead of THROW for error reporting.
PRINT outputs buffered diagnostic text rather than structured logging or error handling.
Business identifier o.CustomerID = 1 is hard-coded directly in the query instead of being parameterized.
Unlabelled date literal '20160101' is embedded directly in the predicate on o.OrderDate.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits an explicit style code and depends on session DATEFORMAT settings.
Using COALESCE on o.CustomerID and i.CustomerID in the JOIN predicate prevents efficient index-based join strategies.
Sales.Orders is self-joined on OrderID solely to select o.OrderID, which is already available without the join.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts all rows of Sales.Orders by an unselective nvarchar(MAX) column.
SUM(ol.Quantity) aggregates the entire Sales.OrderLines table without a restrictive WHERE filter.
The row-level predicate ol.OrderID > 0 is placed in HAVING rather than filtering rows earlier in WHERE.
ORDER BY OrderCount is unnecessary because SELECT COUNT(*) without GROUP BY always returns a single row.
MERGE on Sales.Orders is prone to concurrency and correctness edge cases compared to explicit UPDATE/INSERT logic.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments modifies no data while still acquiring locks and generating transaction log overhead.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 uses a broad non-key value predicate.
WAITFOR DELAY blocks the executing worker thread and holds session resources unnecessarily.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is executed outside a TRY...CATCH block, risking unhandled errors leaving transactions open.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON alters session state and introduces fragile explicit identity management.
Calling sp_who without a schema qualifier forces unnecessary resolution overhead.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 changes a session-level row limit setting and never restores it to 0.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (...) omits an explicit column list, making the insert fragile to column order or schema changes.
LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' begins with a leading wildcard, preventing an index seek on Sales.Customers.CustomerName.
User input parameter @CustomerName is concatenated directly into dynamic SQL string @sql, creating a SQL injection vulnerability.
EXEC sp_executesql @sql runs dynamic SQL without parameterized inputs.
sp_executesql is invoked without the sys schema qualifier.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers has no WHERE clause and will overwrite CustomerCategoryID on every row in the table.
Filtering outer-joined table Sales.Orders in WHERE (o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01') eliminates NULL-extended rows and converts the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than true; IS NULL must be used to match NULL values.
Calling scalar UDF dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the SELECT list forces row-by-row evaluation across Sales.Customers and inhibits parallelism.
The CATCH block handles an error inside an explicit transaction on #DemoCustomers without rolling back the transaction.
The CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE() and neither rethrows with THROW nor returns an error status.
Hardcoding WITH (INDEX = 1) on Sales.Customers prevents the query optimizer from choosing better access paths and breaks if index IDs change.
The query nests four levels of derived-table subqueries on Sales.Customers, reducing readability and maintainability.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' uses a leading wildcard, preventing an index seek on UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti couples the caller to all columns returned by the function.
Querying multi-statement TVF dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti prevents query inlining and often causes poor cardinality estimates compared to an inline TVF.
